source.title: ExPLAIND: Unifying Model, Data, and Training Attribution to Study Model Behavior
source.authors: Florian Eichin; Yu-Pei Du; Philipp Mondorf; M. Matveev; Barbara Plank; Michael A. Hedderich

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies a modulo-addition grokking run and its learning mechanisms using ExPLAIND influence decompositions and layer interventions, rather than reproducing the original study’s method.
record.gate_note: The modulo-addition accuracy trajectory and the paper’s own mechanism measurements and interventions are included. The EuroLLM results describe loss-attribution phases but do not report delayed generalization. Dataset-size, efficiency, and artifact claims mentioned through related work are not results of this study.
record.test_reason: The paper trains the standard modular-addition (mod 113) Transformer and reproduces a grokking curve. It then uses its own influence decomposition plus layer-transplant and layer-swap interventions to probe how the generalizing mechanism forms. Its results bear on V1 (the delay in one setting) and V2 (gradual formation, and the nature of the final phase). The EuroLLM case study reports loss-attribution phases, not delayed generalization, so it does not bear on V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say ExPLAIND's grokking analysis supports previously proposed phases (memorization, then circuit or representation-pipeline formation). They refine the final phase as one where embeddings and outer layers align around that pipeline under high relative regularization influence. They suggest prolonged training reuses and refines existing representations rather than building new ones. They call the study exploratory, note the scores are not causal, and leave generalization to larger models and tasks open.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses an ExPLAIND influence decomposition and layer interventions to analyze a modulo-addition grokking run; it is not presented as a replication of the original training experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The effect of initialization depends on which grokked checkpoint or components are used: earlier pipeline initialization gives rapid generalization but slightly lower final accuracy; attention-only initialization also produces rapid generalization.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), PMLR 306
record.problems: The grokking case study uses one modulo-addition Transformer and one stated training-set size, so it does not establish the dataset-size/delay relationship. The authors describe the case study as exploratory and note that generalization to larger models and more complex tasks remains future work. The causal status of ExPLAIND scores is limited: the paper says they are not designed to provide causal explanations.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant grokking or delayed-generalization results omitted. CNN pruning and data-attribution experiments, and EuroLLM loss-attribution phases, do not test the listed grokking versions.

untested.parts: Whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks: only one split is used (4000 train / 2000 test of 6328 pairs). Only one run is shown for the main curve.
Whether a continuous progress measure quantitatively anticipates the test jump; no excluded/restricted-loss-style metric is reported. Direct measurement of memorizing components being removed.
Not tested: no non-algorithmic grokking, and no initialization-scale or weight-norm manipulation.
Not tested: EuroLLM phases concern loss attribution, not delayed generalization.
Not tested: weight decay is fixed at 4.0, with no critical dataset size and no ungrokking. The link to the efficiency account is only the authors' interpretation.
Not tested: no comparison of algorithms across runs or architectures.
Not tested: no optimizer or numerical-precision controls.

missing.what: Per-checkpoint transplant results: pipelines from steps 339, 539, 1139, 1539, 1739, 1839 and 1939, crossed with component sets (Att., Att.+Lin1, Emb.+Lin2+Dec.), mean of 5 runs. These show from which step the transplanted components already generalize, which bears directly on when the generalizing circuit forms.

Onset of cyclic influence patterns around steps 450–500, well before the test-accuracy jump. Also the Lasso fit showing a dominant cosine component (frequency '113' coefficient 0.112, others under 0.01) in late similarity.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is not an original source. The grokking run is a single configuration taken from Varma et al. (2023). The influence scores are explicitly 'not designed to provide causal explanations'; the causal evidence comes from transplant and swap ablations. The connection the authors draw to the efficiency account is interpretive only, so V5 is not tested. The EuroLLM two-phase finding is not delayed generalization and is correctly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: Whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks; only one training-set size is tested.

The study measures and intervenes on representation-pipeline components and influence phases, but does not establish that its influence scores predict the test-accuracy jump in advance or directly measure removal of memorizing components.
No non-algorithmic grokking-like delay is tested, nor are initialization scale or weight norm varied to switch such a delay on or off.
EuroLLM pretraining loss-attribution dynamics are studied, but delayed generalization during realistic large-model training is not measured.
The study does not test whether weight decay selects a more efficient circuit, nor a critical dataset size or ungrokking.
The study does not compare whether runs converge to the same algorithm across architectures or hyperparameters.
The study does not test whether optimizer or numerical artifacts cause the delay.

rows.value: remains close to zero during the early high-training-accuracy phase, then increases to 100% at step 1939
rows.note: The paper describes the delayed rise; the chance accuracy is not stated.

rows.subject: Transformer model (modulo addition)
rows.size_stated: Single-layer encoder; hidden dimension 64; MLP latent dimension 512
rows.operation_detail: Decomposed prediction influence into kernel and regularization contributions over training
rows.value: Both grow from around epoch 200 and peak near step 1700 before declining; regularization influence dominates in the final phase
rows.note: Authors interpret the final phase as having higher relative regularization influence.
rows.check: These are influence magnitudes, not a direct measure of memorizing components being removed. Late regularization dominance fits a cleanup or regularization-driven final phase, but it does not show removal of memorization.

rows.subject: Transformer model (modulo addition), initialized with grokked components
rows.size_stated: Single-layer encoder; hidden dimension 64; MLP latent dimension 512
rows.operation_detail: Initialized the Attention and Linear-1 layers from grokked counterparts and the remaining parameters randomly
rows.baseline: usual training includes a memorization phase
rows.value: instant generalization within the first 200 training steps, bypassing the usual memorization phase
rows.note: This is a deliberate initialization intervention, not evidence of uninduced behavior in other models.
rows.check: The transplant uses components from the final grokked model. This shows those components carry the generalizing solution, but not that they formed gradually before the jump. It is a deliberate intervention.

rows.subject: Transformer model (modulo addition), initialized with grokked components
rows.size_stated: Single-layer encoder; hidden dimension 64; MLP latent dimension 512
rows.operation_detail: Initialized from an earlier checkpoint’s intermediate representation pipeline, with other parameters random
rows.value: rapid generalization, with slightly lower final accuracy than starting from later checkpoints
rows.note: The text reports this as an earlier-checkpoint initialization.
rows.check: The reader's 'partial' is wrong for V2. Transplanting the step-1539 pipeline gives rapid generalization with only slightly lower final accuracy. This shows the generalizing pipeline was largely formed before test accuracy finished rising, which is what V2 describes. The authors read it as 'continuous refinement of the representation pipeline'.

relationships.condition: Gradual formation of the generalizing mechanism before the test jump, in the mod-113 Transformer
relationships.reason: Middle-layer influence peaks and cyclic influence patterns emerge after memorization and refine continuously. Pipelines transplanted from pre-jump checkpoints (step 1539, attention only) already yield rapid generalization, and outer-layer swaps improve intermediate checkpoints (R5, R7, R9, R10, R11).
relationships.display_finding: Cyclic influence patterns emerge after memorization and refine continuously; attention transplanted from step 1,539 already enables rapid generalization, while outer-layer swaps improve intermediate checkpoints.

source_check.condition: Gradual formation of the generalizing mechanism before the test jump, in the mod-113 Transformer
source_check.reason: R5 and R7 track evolving layer influences and cyclic geometry; R9–R11 provide intervention evidence that a useful pipeline exists before final generalization. This supports the gradual-formation part of V2.

relationships.reason: The final phase appears as embedding/decoder alignment around an already-formed pipeline under high regularization influence, not as directly measured removal of memorization. The authors frame this as refining Nanda et al.'s cleanup stage (R3, R6, R12).
relationships.display_finding: Under strong regularization influence, embeddings and decoder aligned around an already formed pipeline, refining the cleanup interpretation without directly measuring removal of memorizing components.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: R3, R6, and R12 describe regularization influence and outer-layer alignment but do not test removal of identified memorizing components. Alignment does not establish that removal is absent or incomplete; the authors also suggest suppression of inefficient memorization solutions.

relation.reason: The study reports its own delayed-generalization trajectory and interventions testing the formation and functional availability of a generalizing representation pipeline.

tranche.reason: Influence decomposition, checkpoint transplantation, and layer swapping investigate grokking mechanisms through a different method in the established modular-addition setting.

source_check.notes: Direct memorization-component removal and dataset-size dependence are untested. Figure 11 reports transplantation results over five runs, with means and standard deviations.

statements.correction: Final phase: outer-layer alignment around a previously formed representation pipeline under high relative regularization influence. Direct removal of identified memorizing components: untested. Authors additionally suggest regularization suppresses inefficient memorization solutions.
statements.problem: The alignment account and absence of direct memorization-removal measurements are accurate. Treating this study as limits_scope is unsupported: it does not establish that memorization removal fails or that alignment excludes it.
